title: The RBI Is About to Hand the Government Up to ₹3 Lakh Crore. Here’s Why That Number Matters to Every NRI Sending Money Home.
excerpt: The central bank’s board meets May 22 to approve what economists expect to be the largest surplus transfer in Indian history — a windfall driven by a weak dollar, surging gold prices, and aggressive forex interventions.
body:
The Reserve Bank of India’s board meets in Mumbai on Friday to decide on what could be the largest surplus transfer in the central bank’s history. Economists expect the payout to land between ₹2.7 lakh crore and ₹3 lakh crore — potentially surpassing last year’s already record ₹2.68 lakh crore transfer by a significant margin.

The government has budgeted ₹3.16 lakh crore in FY27 from dividends of state-owned enterprises and the RBI combined. If the central bank delivers at the top end of projections, it would cover almost the entire target in a single transfer — a fiscal lifeline at a time when the Indian economy is navigating US tariffs, elevated inflation, and rising import costs.

## What’s Driving the Windfall

Two factors have supercharged the RBI’s accounting profitability this year. First, the US dollar depreciated nearly 10 per cent against major currencies in FY26, boosting the rupee value of the RBI’s massive foreign exchange reserves. Second, gold prices surged approximately 60 per cent during the same period, inflating the value of the central bank’s gold holdings.

The RBI also conducted significant foreign exchange market interventions during the year, buying and selling dollars to manage the rupee’s trajectory. Gross dollar sales reached $166 billion through February 2026, generating trading profits that feed into the surplus. The West Asia crisis in March likely pushed dollar sales even higher in the final weeks of the fiscal year.

The final payout depends on a crucial technical variable: where the RBI sets its Contingent Risk Buffer (CRB). Under the revised Economic Capital Framework, the buffer must be maintained between 4.5 per cent and 7.5 per cent of the balance sheet. Last year, the RBI kept it at the upper end — 7.5 per cent. If Governor Sanjay Malhotra’s board opts to lower the buffer even modestly, the transfer could exceed ₹3 lakh crore.

## The Projections

Sakshi Gupta, principal economist at HDFC Bank, estimates ₹2.8 lakh crore, assuming a CRB of 6.5 per cent. Barclays expects ₹3 lakh crore. Emkay has projected a wider range of ₹2.8 to ₹3.4 lakh crore, depending on the buffer decision. On the more conservative end, Gaura Sengupta, chief economist at IDFC First Bank, expects the payout to remain broadly in line with last year, noting that earnings from foreign exchange transactions were actually lower than in FY25, when gross dollar sales were nearly $400 billion.

## What It Means for NRIs

For the diaspora, the RBI dividend is not an abstraction — it feeds directly into the government’s fiscal capacity, which in turn affects the rupee’s stability, sovereign credit ratings, and the attractiveness of Indian fixed-income investments.

A larger-than-expected transfer would ease fiscal deficit pressure, potentially keeping the rupee in a tighter range and reducing the risk of a credit rating downgrade — both of which matter for NRIs holding rupee-denominated assets, NRI fixed deposits, or remittance-dependent families. India received $129 billion in remittances in 2025, the highest of any country, and the rupee’s trajectory directly affects the purchasing power of every dollar or pound sent home.

Conversely, if the RBI keeps the buffer high and the transfer disappoints, markets could react negatively, adding pressure to a rupee that has already been under strain from elevated crude oil prices and the US tariff shock.

## The Bigger Picture

The RBI’s dividend transfers have quietly become one of the government’s most important fiscal tools. Over the past three years, the central bank has transferred more than ₹7 lakh crore to the exchequer — a trend that critics argue creates an unhealthy dependence on monetary authority profits to plug fiscal gaps.

For now, the market consensus is optimistic. Bond markets have already priced in a large transfer, and a positive surprise could trigger a rally in Indian government securities. The board meets at 10 AM on Friday. By the time most NRIs wake up, the number will be out — and it will shape fiscal expectations for the rest of the year.
